lesson.title: When Disasters Don't Care How Crowded You Are
lesson.summary: Density-independent factors, mainly severe weather and natural disturbances, reduce populations by roughly the same proportion regardless of how crowded the population already was, unlike density-dependent factors.
lesson.body:
Not every limiting factor cares how many individuals are packed into a habitat. A density-independent factor affects roughly the same fraction of a population no matter what its density is. A hard freeze, a severe drought, a hurricane, a wildfire, or a volcanic eruption tends to kill or displace a similar proportion of a population whether that population started out small or large. Contrast that with the density-dependent factors from the previous chapter: competition for food gets worse specifically because a population is crowded, but a sudden cold snap does not become gentler just because a population happens to be sparse.

A simple way to picture the difference: imagine an insect population that experiences an unusually hard frost. If the frost kills roughly the same percentage of individuals whether the population going in was small or enormous, that is the signature of a density-independent effect. Compare that to a scenario where crowding itself drives up disease transmission or starvation, so that a much larger fraction of a dense population dies than would die in a sparse one, which is the signature of density dependence instead. Weather events, along with other abiotic disturbances like floods and fires, are the textbook examples of factors that behave the first way.

This distinction is genuinely useful for predicting how populations will respond to different kinds of stress, but it is worth being cautious about treating it as a perfectly clean division. Real populations often experience both kinds of pressure at once, and they can interact. A population already weakened by crowding and food scarcity, for instance, may be more vulnerable to a cold snap than a well fed, low density population would be, even though the cold snap itself is not caused by density. So while density-dependent and density-independent factors are a genuinely useful way to organize how ecologists think about what regulates populations, most real world population changes reflect some mix of both, rather than a pure case of one or the other.
